title: Frontend Testing and Accessibility
learning_outcomes: Explain component testing in the context of frontend testing and accessibility.
Apply the lesson concept in a small TypeScript example and describe what the compiler can check.
Identify one limitation or failure case and choose an appropriate runtime check or test when needed.

content.intro: Learn frontend testing and accessibility through a compact mental model, syllabus-aligned subtopics, a worked example and a practical task. The goal is not to memorize syntax but to know what the type contract guarantees and what evidence is still needed.
content.why_it_matters: Framework and service APIs vary by version. Keep application/domain models separate from transport input, validate untrusted data at runtime, and test the behavior that sits behind each type contract.

content_blocks.title: Mental model
content_blocks.text: **Frontend Testing and Accessibility.** This lesson belongs to **Frontend Development with TypeScript**. Start by identifying the problem that frontend testing and accessibility solves. In TypeScript, separate three questions: what values your program intends to accept, what the compiler can prove from the code, and what must still be checked while the program runs. The last category matters whenever data comes from a user, file, API, storage layer, or an untyped JavaScript dependency.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics and how to use them

items.title: Component testing
items.text: For component testing, define observable acceptance criteria and test both expected behavior and a failure case. Preserve a small regression test for any bug or inference problem you fix.

items.title: Semantic HTML and accessible events
items.text: For semantic html and accessible events, write down the input contract and the result contract. Let TypeScript infer obvious local types, and add annotations where they clarify a public API, callback, or boundary.

items.title: Typed test utilities
items.text: For typed test utilities, define observable acceptance criteria and test both expected behavior and a failure case. Preserve a small regression test for any bug or inference problem you fix.

content_blocks.title: Compile-time versus runtime
content_blocks.text: Type annotations and most type declarations are erased when TypeScript emits JavaScript. They do not validate external JSON, authorize a user, sanitize HTML, or prevent runtime failures by themselves. Validate trust-boundary inputs and test the behavior.

content.task: Create a small TypeScript example for “Frontend Testing and Accessibility”. Demonstrate component testing, explain your assumption, and include one check that shows the expected behavior. Do not treat a type annotation as runtime validation for external input.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one syllabus subtopic named in this lesson.
The type contract is explicit enough that another learner can explain what it accepts and rejects.
The learner records a failure case and distinguishes compile-time checks from runtime validation.
hints: Start with the syllabus item “Component testing” and define the smallest example that demonstrates it.
Ask which part is checked by TypeScript and which part depends on runtime data, the environment or a test.
For external input, start with unknown and validate the required shape before using a domain type.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a successful type check as a runtime guarantee.
common_mistakes.why: Type annotations do not generally validate data after JavaScript starts running.
common_mistakes.fix: Add runtime checks for external input and tests for meaningful failure cases.

common_mistakes.problem: Using any or an assertion to silence a useful diagnostic.
common_mistakes.why: That can hide the exact mismatch the type system would otherwise report.
common_mistakes.fix: Prefer a more precise type or unknown plus narrowing; use assertions only when a verified invariant justifies them.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a compiler setting or runtime example without checking the project environment.
common_mistakes.why: Module resolution, DOM/Node globals, JSX and tool behavior depend on the configured versions and environment.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin the toolchain, match tsconfig to the runtime/bundler, and run the actual project's typecheck and tests.

summary: Frontend Testing and Accessibility is taught through the subtopics listed in the source syllabus: Component testing, Semantic HTML and accessible events, Typed test utilities.
Prefer precise contracts and use compiler diagnostics as evidence, not as a replacement for runtime tests.
Validate untrusted data and describe environment/version assumptions explicitly.
